description: Ten assistant-rewritten, task-general classification instructions with diverse strategies: minimal matching, hypothesis challenge, elimination, temporal analysis, attribution and scope, holistic interpretation, competing cases, optional example analogy, counterfactual evidence checking, and an evidence table. Existing IDs retained. Label names, label count, and domain criteria are supplied by the task template. All current wording is assistant-generated; transfer performance and behavioral diversity remain to be evaluated.

prompts.instruction: Choose the label that best matches the text under the supplied definitions. Return only the label.

Start with the most plausible label as a working hypothesis. Identify its strongest supporting evidence, then actively look for contradictions and evidence favoring other labels. Revise the hypothesis when another definition fits better. Do not treat missing evidence as confirmation. Output only the final label.

Use elimination before commitment. Compare the text against each supplied definition and rule out labels contradicted by decisive evidence. Missing information alone does not justify elimination. Compare the remaining candidates using their distinguishing criteria; if every label was eliminated, recheck your assumptions. Return the single best-supported label.

Organize relevant events and claims by time: earlier circumstances, the present situation, changes, and future expectations. Distinguish actual events from imagined, conditional, or anticipated ones. Use temporal distinctions only where they matter to the supplied label definitions; if timing is irrelevant, decide from the remaining evidence. Output only the selected label.

Resolve attribution and scope before classifying. Identify who makes each claim, whom or what it concerns, and whether it is asserted, quoted, questioned, denied, or hypothetical. Use these distinctions to avoid assigning evidence to the wrong subject or treating a denial as an assertion. Apply the supplied definitions and output only the label.

Interpret the text as a coherent whole. Consider how contrasts, qualifications, and context change the meaning of individual phrases. Choose the supplied label that best captures the overall interpretation while respecting any decisive criterion in its definition. Do not substitute an unrelated classification scheme. Return only the label.

Compare competing cases for the available labels. For each plausible label, identify the strongest supporting detail and the strongest objection grounded in the text. Prefer the case that better satisfies the supplied definition with fewer unsupported assumptions. Keep the comparison internal and return only the selected label.

When labeled examples are supplied, compare their evidence patterns with those of the input rather than relying on shared vocabulary or topic. Check whether the similarities and differences matter under the label definitions. If no examples are supplied, compare directly with the definitions without inventing examples. Return only the best-fitting label.

Make a provisional decision, then identify the evidence that distinguishes it from competing labels. Consider whether removing that evidence would change the decision and whether the evidence is actually relevant to a supplied criterion. Check that incidental details are not driving the choice. Make the final classification on the complete original text and return only its label.

Build an internal evidence table linking relevant statements to the supplied label criteria, including their subject, certainty, and any contradictions. Consolidate repetition unless frequency itself is part of a criterion. Compare the evidence patterns across the available labels; absence of a statement does not prove its opposite. Output only the chosen label, not the table.
